newsitem.title: USA: McKinney accuser testifies at sex harassment hearing.
newsitem.headline: McKinney accuser testifies at sex harassment hearing.

text.p: A retired Army officer who first accused Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney of sexual harassment said on Friday she felt degraded when he propositioned her while on a business trip to Hawaii last year.
"It was the most embarrassing, degrading (experience) I have ever had to go through in my entire life," retired Sgt. Maj. Brenda Hoster said at a military hearing. "I didn't know what to do."

Hoster said McKinney came to her hotel room in Hawaii in April 1996, kissed her, lifted her off her feet and at one point said, "I could take you right here, right now." Hoster said she understood that to mean he could have had her sexually.

McKinney then urged her to look at his groin area, Hoster said. "Don't you want to look and see what you did to me?" Hoster quoted McKinney as saying. She said she thought he was referring to an erection.
Hoster said she told McKinney to leave her room and go to his wife, who was in another hotel room. McKinney eventually left, Hoster said.

McKinney, a 29-year Army veteran and the highest-ranking enlisted soldier, is charged with sexual misconduct involving five military women. He has vehemently denied all charges. The current hearing will determine if McKinney will be court- martialed.

Hoster's testimony is important because she was McKinney's first accuser, filing an official complaint with the Army last January after she had retired as a sergeant major and an officer on McKinney's public relations staff.
Hoster said she confronted McKinney before she retired in November, and said McKinney apologised for his behaviour on the Hawaii trip.
"He told me it had been bothering him too, that he had no excuses, that he wasn't proud of it and he actually cried," Hoster said.
She said she would have retired quietly and not filed any complaint against McKinney had he not taken a position on an official Army panel investigating charges of sexual harassment.

"I wrote him a letter in early December (1996)," she testified. "I told him that I couldn't believe he allowed himself to be put on this panel ... I told him, you're guilty of the behaviour you're investigating." She urged him either to leave the panel or retire from the Army.

She said she had gone to other Army officials to address the problem, and twice called a special hotline for reporting sexual harassment in the military, but never gave her name because she expected someone of McKinney's rank would be shielded.
"I didn't trust the system ... The higher up you are (in rank), the more you get protected," Hoster said.

In earlier hearing sessions, witnesses have portrayed McKinney as a man who pursued sex even after several rejections, using his powerful post as a threat against their careers. One woman said she had unwanted sex with McKinney while she was nearly eight months pregnant.
Hoster, who had originally been reluctantly to testify, agreed after receiving assurances that defence lawyers would be restricted in questioning her about her own sex life.
Hoster's lawyer, Susan Barnes, has said that earlier hearing sessions had "a generally abusive atmosphere in which the defence was walking over these victims."
